#34804. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2275 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • Industry observers note that researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • It has been revealed that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Industry observers note that researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

It has been revealed that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

In a recent development, conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," claims Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Sources indicate that although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

It has been revealed that "In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the newly introduced approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Industry observers note that crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

It has been revealed that the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the upcoming research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

In a recent development, this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

Industry observers note that the researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is vital because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Sources indicate that whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

Sources indicate that the nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

In a recent development, the weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

Industry observers note that these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

Industry observers note that this makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain notable challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

Sources indicate that from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study highlights how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising latest way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Recent findings suggest that every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

Recent findings suggest that we tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

In a recent development, most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the fresh text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:.

It has been revealed that one help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:.

In a recent development, each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:.

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

Industry observers note that langSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation notes you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:.

Recent findings suggest that those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Sources indicate that labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the latest version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

According to recent reports, langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:.

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation demonstrates only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:.

In a recent development, that is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

It has been revealed that errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Recent findings suggest that size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change highlighted up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:.

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:.

According to recent reports, the rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

According to recent reports, putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

In a recent development, A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Recent findings suggest that keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

In a recent development, use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Industry observers note that use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Sources indicate that use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per newly introduced set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

#34800. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1530 w)

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • In a recent development, but position and time are different.
  • In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

In a recent development, but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Sources indicate that understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

Sources indicate that however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

In a recent development, at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

It has been revealed that tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with key changes taking place over just attoseconds.

To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Sources indicate that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

According to recent reports, to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a newly introduced laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

Sources indicate that the researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Industry observers note that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It indicated that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

According to recent reports, their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become key simultaneously.

According to recent reports, for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

In a recent development, the team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

It has been revealed that raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a latest aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

It has been revealed that transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the presently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

Industry observers note that that possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a upcoming foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

#34796. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a upcoming form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," states Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

In a recent development, the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an crucial role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are at the moment beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

Sources indicate that in the fresh system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Recent findings suggest that many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Recent findings suggest that mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

According to recent reports, another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Recent findings suggest that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

In a recent development, "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Industry observers note that successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments revealed that the fresh architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

According to recent reports, one of the most significant findings is that the fresh system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

In a recent development, however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Industry observers note that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

In a recent development, practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising fresh route toward making those machines a reality.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over the past five days, a string of high-profile tech outages has left Americans struggling to send emails, catch flights, and access their bank accounts. While the disruptions raised concerns about AI-powered cybersecurity threats, the real culprit may be something less sinister: corporate America’s tech systems are simply out of date. Outages like those at JPMorgan Chase, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and Microsoft can occur when computer systems are undergoing major upgrades, Marva Bailer, CEO of tech advisory firm Qualaix, told the Fresh York Post. Bolting on new technology can leave the systems vulnerable. Although it is unclear whether the recent outages were directly related to artificial intelligence, many organizations are at the moment upgrading their networks to handle AI tools. Microsoft attributed its outage to an problem that arose during a network capacity upgrade, according to the Financial Times. The time of year could also be a factor, as technicians rush to make sure systems are ready for the holiday shopping and travel season. “It’s holiday time, it’s travel time, it’s shopping,” Bailer told the New York Post. “So, you have all those higher spikes in volume and more pressure to [revision your systems].” AI is also allowing companies to identify software vulnerabilities far more rapidly, possibly leaving IT workers with too much work on their hands, the Post reported. Like Bailer, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to companies trying to upgrade aging systems, during an appearance on CNBC earlier today. “[They’re] pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system,” he said. The disruptions serve as a reminder of how cutting-edge technology is often still dependent on centralized, aging systems. Friday’s nationwide ground stop, which resulted in more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days, was triggered by the installation of a single router at a remote facility in Arkansas, Reuters reported. Monday’s software glitch at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions for customers of other major banks, even though their own computer systems were functioning normally. Indeed, third-party tech providers have accounted for roughly two-thirds of publicly reported IT outages over the past nine years, according to a recent report from Uptime Institute, a global digital infrastructure advisory firm based in New York City.

Breaking: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A fresh computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A fresh computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

In a recent development, these imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Recent findings suggest that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez remarked. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Light plays an notable role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez mentioned.

Industry observers note that beyond identifying latest candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for fresh medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

According to recent reports, the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he stated. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if Instagram is your preferred avenue for media consumption, you’ve probably come across posts by Impact.
  • If Instagram is your preferred avenue for media consumption, you’ve probably come across posts by Impact.
  • Launched in 2020 by founders Tim Chau and Michelle Andrews, the Impact Instagram handle was born in the apex of Gen Z’s formative years, an era marked by a hyper-online generation who reckoned with Donald Trump, COVID-19, social isolation, canceled graduations, the murder of George Floyd, and climate disaster all in the same year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if Instagram is your preferred avenue for media consumption, you’ve probably come across posts by Impact. The popular Gen-Z-targeted account is characterized by its quick-turn analysis on progressive, left-wing topics ranging from identity politics to mental health and niche internet trends. That winning formula caught the attention of social video publisher NowThis, which recently acquired the brand. Debuted in 2020 by founders Tim Chau and Michelle Andrews, the Impact Instagram handle was born in the apex of Gen Z’s formative years, an era marked by a hyper-online generation who reckoned with Donald Trump, COVID-19, social isolation, canceled graduations, the murder of George Floyd, and climate disaster all in the same year. Impact created timely stories around narratives that Gen Z desperately craved and traditional media often failed to cover: Its content is often among the first to share pointed commentary on trending headlines. When comedian Shane Gillis was being criticized online for a misogynistic SNL bit, Impact published “Male comedians don’t actually have to hate women to be popular.” After the internet was in an uproar over the U.K. banning books authored by Sally Rooney due to her support for Palestine, Impact wrote about it immediately. Impact even creates content around shared woes that span multiple generations, helping it reach larger audiences—as seen in posts like “Is it rude to ask friends to stay with them when you visit their city?” The comments section of each post is the heart of the community the Impact team has built and a glimpse into real cultural capital, making it easy to see why NowThis chose to purchase the manufacturer. Founded in 2012 by former Huffington Post execs Kenneth Lerer and Eric Hippeau, NowThis began as a social-first go-to for millennial content before being acquired by Vox Media. As millennials aged into the next phase of adulthood, companies and news organizations from all corners of the internet competed for the coveted attention of young people, nudging the video publisher into a new chapter. In 2023, NowThis expanded into a large-scale media network targeting Gen Z, taking on a new CEO, Sharon Mussalli, and a new editor-in-chief, Michael Vito Valentino, while also reckoning with the ramifications of significant layoffs. This latest move in acquiring Impact—for an alleged seven-figure all-cash deal—demonstrates a commitment to reaching its target audience and the community of young people behind Impact. “[They] care about what’s happening in the world and want to understand how it connects to their relationships, their work, their culture, and their futures. That’s closely aligned with the Gen Z female audience we’re building for at NowThis. And we saw an opportunity to invest in that relationship and give it more room to grow,” Mussalli noted in a statement via the NowThis PR team. She adds: “Impact brings a distinct editorial voice and a strong sense of what resonates with its community. We bring the production capabilities and experience developing original video franchises to help translate that into new series and recurring formats. Our ambition is to build something this audience can grow with, across all NowThis channels. That means giving people more than an individual story they encounter in their feed—it means creating recognizable programming they seek out, share, and return to.”  In a statement to Fast Company, Chau, who is stepping down from the Impact staff but will remain involved in some capacity, calls the move “bittersweet.” “We put everything into Impact to get it where it is today, so stepping back isn’t easy. But we couldn’t be happier about where it’s headed, because we know NowThis is the right home for it. They’re leading in a space where social now dominates—really the first of their kind—and that’s exactly the future we want Impact to be part of.” “My hope is that Impact stays the place young people go to for stories that actually land with them, the ones they talk about with friends, share, and sit with. Legacy media has struggled to resonate with this generation, and I hope Impact can keep being the place where they feel truly understood and connected,” Chau said.

#34787. A newly introduced report says free childcare in NYC will pay for itself

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1366 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

A newly introduced report says free childcare in NYC will pay for itself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that since taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made it his mission to expand access to affordable childcare in the city, and for good reason.
  • Since taking office, Latest York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made it his mission to expand access to affordable childcare in the city, and for good reason.
  • A upcoming report reveals how universal childcare would not only benefit families in New York City, but also boost the economy: Just 35 hours of free childcare per week could bring up to $6.5 billion in economic value each year, which would likely exceed the cost of providing that care.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that since taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made it his mission to expand access to affordable childcare in the city, and for good reason. On average, NYC families spend $21,000 on childcare annually per child—equaling an estimated $10 billion citywide every year. While about 40% of children in the city receive some free or subsidized care, the remaining 60% receive none, leaving many families to pay entirely out of pocket. A new report reveals how universal childcare would not only benefit families in New York City, but also boost the economy: Just 35 hours of free childcare per week could bring up to $6.5 billion in economic value each year, which would likely exceed the cost of providing that care. The report—which was produced by a nonpartisan think tank, the 5BORO Institute at Citizens Union, in partnership with Boston Consulting Group—surveyed more than 2,700 parents of children younger than 5, along with about a hundred families who moved away from New York City recently. According to the report, nearly 70% of children under the age of 6 are cared for by parents or adults who work. When those parents are unable to find care and forced to drop out of the workforce or switch jobs, the city loses $1.7 billion in annual income; among the parents surveyed, 15% altered their work situation due to childcare issues. For hourly workers, childcare gaps can force them to miss out on $360 million in earnings each year. The report also found that childcare was a leading concern for families who had left the city, a growing trend that is supported by plenty of other data. In other words, employers also feel the effects of inadequate access to care. That can mean high turnover or simply lost productivity if their workers regularly contend with disruptions to their childcare: More than half of the parents surveyed remarked they had missed at least one full day of work over the past three months, averaging three to four missed days. These childcare gaps can cost New York City employers about 54 million hours of missed work, according to the report. The act of providing 35 hours of free childcare each week would also enable nearly 30,000 parents to reenter the workforce, which could yield more than a billion dollars in annual earnings. Childcare has been a key focus for Mamdani since his campaign, and as Fast Tech giant reported in a recent cover story, the mayor has even gotten the business community on board with its investments in this area. Mamdani is already building upon the universal 3-K program established by former Mayor Bill de Blasio to extend care to younger children; the recently introduced 2-K program is now providing free, full-day childcare to 2,000 2-year-olds, with intends to serve an additional 10,000 children by next fall. (The city has provided free pre-K to all 4-year-olds since 2014.)  Even business leaders who are critical of Mamdani have seemingly come around to the idea of free childcare, though they may not agree on how to achieve that. This fall, the 5BORO Institute created the NYC Child Care Business Council, bringing together a number of business leaders and organizations committed to putting their muscle behind this matter and advocating for childcare investment (something the business community has not historically done). For years, employers have invested in generous parental leave policies and backup childcare benefits for their workforce to help them court top talent and retain some of their best employees. But it seems companies are finally realizing that their best efforts can’t make up for a lack of robust childcare options or offset the mounting cost of care. “The market is not able to solve this problem,” Grace Rauh, the executive director of Citizens Union, recently told Fast Company. Citizens Union is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded in 1897 to promote government accountability, ethics, transparency, and civic engagement across New York. “Frankly, private businesses aren’t able to provide the kind of fully robust childcare benefits that their employees need,” Rauh said.

#34785. Latest Update: Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1608 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang had one message: It’s business as usual

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings call in its 33-year history without cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
  • Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings call in its 33-year history without cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
  • Analysts wanted to know what the firm would say about the succession initiative after Huang’s departure, and about the future of Nvidia’s pivotal role as the company powering the AI race.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia on Tuesday held its first earnings call in its 33-year history without cofounder Jensen Huang, who resigned five days ago after a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. After reporting strong third-quarter numbers, interim CEO Colette Kress (who has been Nvidia’s CFO since 2013) kept the call focused on Nvidia’s immediate business concerns. Analysts wanted to know what the organization would say about the succession initiative after Huang’s departure, and about the future of Nvidia’s pivotal role as the company powering the AI race. Most of the salient information about Huang was given at the front of the call by Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair of the board. Jones mentioned Nvidia doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO, providing a clapback to the growing contingent on social media lobbying for the ousted CEO’s return. Jones said the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles is handling the search for a fresh CEO, but that Nvidia is looking at both internal and external candidates for the job. “The board is acting deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees and investors,” Jones said. “With that we will take no further questions about the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.” The numbers Kress then took over the call and kept things focused on Nvidia’s numbers. Kress has run Nvidia’s earnings calls for years, but always alongside Huang, who set the company’s vision and did much of its dealmaking with customers and partners. Today her main job was to report the quarterly numbers, and convince investors that the world’s most key AI chip company can run without its founder. The numbers, at least, are good. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for its fiscal third quarter, well above Wall Street’s roughly $109 billion forecast, and projected $130 billion for the current quarter. Investors expected a beat. Kress said Nvidia has seen “explosive” adoption of its latest Vera Rubin computing platform, which includes a Rubin GPU and a Vera CPU. “Our momentum is real,” she said. “Our ambition will not change, our passion for innovation will not change.”  Revenue for the quarter came in at $115.8 billion, about $6.5 billion higher than the roughly $109 billion analysts expected. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 per share, 21 cents above the $2.47 consensus. But all that happened during a third quarter that ended October 25—that is, before the Huang scandal broke. That’s why analysts were more concerned about the guidance numbers for a future without Huang. Some analysts had even questioned whether Nvidia would venture to give a full year 2028 guidance. But it did. For the short term, Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. The company had previously said it expects to see 70% growth in 2028, but Kress said its moving that guidance up to 75% growth, citing continued strong demand for AI infrastructure, including Vera Rubin, and despite the chance that chip exports to China will constrict somewhat in the wake of the Huang scandal. That may have settled some analysts’ nerves about the AI sell-off that started in October, which was driven by the fear that Massive Tech companies would slow their spending on AI data centers. Why this call mattered Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, resigned on November 12 amid two scandals. The first involved an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence believe may have been spying for China. Beijing has strongly denied the allegations. Nvidia’s board has opened an internal investigation into whether company or national security secrets were compromised. Huang stepped down shortly after reports of a second alleged affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare (and the CEO’s direct report). The board made Kress interim CEO. She also stays on as CFO until a permanent CEO is named. Longtime director Harvey Jones became Nvidia’s first board chair. The stock was already falling before the scandal. Nvidia closed at a record $239.24 on October 6. Shares then fell on fears that AI spending would slow, and fell further as the Huang story unfolded. By Tuesday the stock was below $154, its lowest level since mid-2025. That’s a loss of about $2 trillion in market value. That’s why Wall Street was listening to Kress so closely. Before the call, analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives predicted Kress would talk very little about Huang, that her main job would be to “restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward,” he told Fox Business. And that’s exactly what happened. After the brief section at the front, the call had a business-as-usual tone, complete with a blizzard of numbers showing that Nvidia—as of the third quarter, at least—continues to sit at the center of the AI world.
