#34783. Industry News: Why the smartest AI strategy starts with a little laziness

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1924 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Why the smartest AI strategy starts with a little laziness

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My employees know that I have an unconventional take on laziness: A lazy mindset doesn’t mean being unproductive.
  • It has been revealed that my employees know that I have an unconventional take on laziness: A lazy mindset doesn’t mean being unproductive.
  • That’s why I encourage a lazy mindset, insofar as it means looking for more efficient ways to get things done—like leveraging the latest AI and automation tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My employees know that I have an unconventional take on laziness: A lazy mindset doesn’t mean being unproductive. Often, it means finding a faster way to get something done. As Bill Gates famously remarked, “I choose a lazy person to do a hard job. Because a lazy person will find an easy way to do it.” That’s why I encourage a lazy mindset, insofar as it means looking for more efficient ways to get things done—like leveraging the latest AI and automation tools. As I’ve seen in leading a company of more than 800 employees, people are eager to streamline their work. Studies confirm they’re doing it, whether their employers know about it or not. One recent report found that while only 40% of companies surveyed had purchased official subscriptions to large language models, employees at more than 90% of those companies reported regular use of artificial intelligence. That often leads to piecemeal adoption and missed opportunities to realize AI’s full potential. Studies suggest AI can absorb 60% to 70% of busywork, freeing employees to focus on more meaningful tasks, like strategizing and coming up with innovative solutions. Leaders should recognize this reality and adopt AI initiatives at the enterprise level. But the challenge isn’t finding opportunities—there are countless AI tools on the market, and more rolling out every day. It’s deciding which are worth pursuing. Every AI initiative comes with trade-offs, requiring time, budget, talent, and executive approval. Here are some tips for taking a more strategic approach to AI adoption in your company. Start with business goals, not AI tools Estimates of the number of AI tools on the market vary widely, from around 2,500 to more than 50,000. (If you look at live, available products, the lower figure is likely more accurate.) But one thing is indisputable: There are a ton, more than anyone could possibly test while working a full-time job. Amid this dizzying array of options, the first step in integrating AI into an organization is top down, clarifying your broader business goals. Maybe your primary objective is to make it easier for users to incorporate your software into their everyday lives. AI-powered chatbots that field recurring user questions could be a wise investment. Or maybe your goal is to analyze users’ circumstances quickly and provide help faster. A tool that uses AI to analyze and synthesize vast amounts of data could transform your business. In healthcare, for example, IBM’s Watson has been used to analyze patient data and medical literature and provide doctors with evidence-based treatment options. The key is to start with the problem you want to solve, not the technology you’re excited to use. When leaders define their business goals, they can focus on AI opportunities that align with those goals and avoid the myriad distractions out there. Rather than dedicating resources to tools that merely speed things up, they can focus on uses with the greatest potential impact. They can deliberately pass on AI tools that don’t align with business objectives and concentrate their efforts where AI can make the biggest difference. Let employees lead the way If you were developing upcoming cooking technology for a bakery, you probably wouldn’t begin with the product designer. You’d start by asking the baker how they work, where things tend to go awry, and how you might improve their processes. The best ideas for improving how people work often come from those on the front lines. At my company, we invite all employees to share the AI tools they’ve discovered that have helped, or could potentially help, during our weekly demo days. It’s a valuable exchange of ideas—for example, customer service reps advising designers on how to better program help chatbots. Experts have observed the power of peer-to-peer learning networks, where employees develop and share ideas for AI adoption. Take an article in Harvard Business Review about AI usage at the European bank BBVA: “Instead of relying on the core IT and operations functions, the organization empowered the people who understood business processes best to design the solutions.” While leaders can create a framework for AI adoption, starting with clear business priorities, they also need to tap employees for their ideas and insights into where and how tools can truly improve internal processes and the customer experience. Whether it’s an online forum, a Slack conversation, or a weekly all-hands meeting, make sure there’s a channel where employees can contribute their perspectives on AI development and share best practices. Make trade-offs deliberately Organization-wide change requires investments of both time and money. That’s why I recommend encouraging employees to build slack into their schedules to test and experiment with new tools and figure out how to streamline their workflows. Each step eliminated, each minute of busywork recaptured makes a difference—and the benefits compound over time. Recognizing that every AI initiative competes for limited time, budget, and attention helps organizations decide where to invest more wisely. Experts recommend managing AI investments like a portfolio, evaluating each one against objective criteria. Consider whether an investment serves broader business goals, whether additional training is needed, what other resources are required, and the cost of diverting those resources. As they assess potential investments, leaders can also track whether their overall AI strategy is delivering returns. As noted in another HBR article, “The goal is to ensure that individual projects advance business strategy and that the overall mix of investments creates sustainable value.” Ultimately, this means being as deliberate about what to deprioritize as what to pursue. Success with AI depends less on which tools companies adopt and more on their willingness to stay focused on the initiatives that matter most. Be lazy about how much you take on, and smart about what you choose.

Consider whether an investment serves broader business goals, whether additional training is needed, what other resources are required, and the cost of diverting those resources. As they assess potential investments, leaders can also track whether their overall AI strategy is delivering returns. As noted in another HBR article, “The goal is to ensure that individual projects advance business strategy and that the overall mix of investments creates sustainable value.”.

Ultimately, this means being as deliberate about what to deprioritize as what to pursue. Success with AI depends less on which tools companies adopt and more on their willingness to stay focused on the initiatives that matter most. Be lazy about how much you take on, and smart about what you choose.

Latest Update: How to clock out psychologically—and leave the bad vibes at work

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to leave work stress where it belongs: at work.
  • It’s hard to leave work stress where it belongs: at work.
  • Recent findings suggest that stressful days spent navigating tense conversations with coworkers or clients, or staring down an endless to-do list or email queue, can cause rumination, anxiety, and even after-hours work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to leave work stress where it belongs: at work. Stressful days spent navigating tense conversations with coworkers or clients, or staring down an endless to-do list or email queue, can cause rumination, anxiety, and even after-hours work. Your job anxiety can easily, and frequently, spill into your personal life. To break the cycle, experts suggest creating a wind-down routine. Understanding Emotional Residue and Rumination Our brains are hardwired to replay unfinished business, which is why you can’t just turn off your thoughts after a tough day at work. Forcing yourself to stop thinking about a stressful situation usually backfires, and this can exacerbate your worry. “Trying not to think about it, generally does not work, as our brains will latch harder onto anything we’re trying to push out,” notes psychologist Meera Khan, clinical director at the mental health treatment manufacturer LifeStance Health in Bensalem, Pennsylvania. Without a solid routine to wrap up your workday, spillover stress easily creeps into dinner time and ruins the rest of your night, according to the Journal of Occupational Health Psychology. “When something upsetting happens at work, the stress doesn’t automatically disappear just because the workday is over,” explains neuropsychologist Sanam Hafeez, director of the neuropsychological assessment practice Comprehend the Mind in Upcoming York. “Your mind will oftentimes replay the moment over and over, trying to make sense of what happened,” she says. To break free from that mental loop, research published in the journal Acta Psychologica highlights a few simple strategies: First, acknowledge how you are feeling. Then, write it down or talk it through with someone. Finally, give yourself permission to step away and leave whatever is unfinished for tomorrow. Simple Routines to Help You Unwind After Work Having a noticeable routine at the end of the day signals your brain that work is over. Heading home used to give us a natural break, but working from home doesn’t give the same type of break. “Commuting is stressful, and it often means packed buses and standing in traffic,” points out Manuela Collis, assistant professor of organization and strategy at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College in Pittsburgh. “But the commute also did something useful for us: It created a temporal and physical boundary between what happens at work and life outside of it,” she says. If there’s no commute, create new ways to wind down on your next WFH day. Stroll outside for a few minutes, walk your dog, or listen to an audiobook or podcast. And then, after you log off, instead of dwelling on work complications all night, set a firm cutoff point and shift your focus to your personal life. “I recommend taking a few minutes at the end of each workday to write down anything that’s bothering you—that way, you have a clear strategy for what to tackle the next day,” suggests Hafeez, who has a PsyD degree in school-community psychology. Another tactic is to create a buffer. Before signing off, take two minutes to write down any worrisome tasks or stressors so they don’t linger in your head all night; putting something on paper can help transition it out of your mind, at least for now. Here are a few other simple ways to bridge the gap between work and your personal time. Change your outfit: Take off your work clothes and put on comfy clothing. Take a 10-minute walk: Unplug, step away from your screen, and get some fresh air. Don’t feel compelled to check email: This one can be hard, given our 24/7 availability and smartphone culture—but the messages will be there tomorrow. So step away for tonight. The science backs this up. Per a study published in Frontiers in Psychology, participants who use such “sensory transition rituals” reduce work-life conflict by nearly half compared with those who are constantly on their devices. And if work stress still manages to sneak back in, it could be helpful to give yourself a finite time to worry. “If you find yourself replaying work stress after hours, ask yourself if the issue is something you can solve right now,” advises Khan, who has a PsyD degree in clinical psychology. “I recommend a simple five-to-10-minute rule: If you can address it in five to 10 minutes, go ahead and do it. If not, let it wait,” she says. Setting Boundaries and Normalizing Recovery Culture As you make the shifts necessary to preserve your health and mental wellness, don’t feel guilty about it. This is time to reclaim your evenings and set boundaries. And when you work remotely, these blurred lines can make it a wee more challenging—especially given our culture of workaholism—but not impossible. “Working from home can make it feel like you’re expected to be available all the time,” Hafeez says. “But being a good employee doesn’t mean you have to be available 24/7.” Physical boundaries matter just as much as mental ones. “If you have the space or privilege to set up a dedicated workspace, try to keep all work-related activities contained to that area,” Khan suggests. Leadership plays a key role, too. Managers need to practice what they preach and show their teams that staying online around the clock isn’t a badge of honor. “To help teams truly disconnect, managers can avoid scheduling late-day meetings, queue emails to send during regular working hours, and be crystal clear about expectations—especially what isn’t expected,” Collis notes. The Bottom Line The bad vibes shouldn’t follow you home; it’s okay to want to have calm evenings. Everyone is telling us to be more mindful and to preserve our headspace, but it isn’t an easy proposition. Clocking out from your work isn’t just about closing your laptop; it’s about creating meaningful and impactful ways to disconnect from work and keep tomorrow out of tonight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC drivers will now be able to unlock their vehicles with their phones. As first reported by MacRumors, General Motors declared that it has begun rolling out the Apple Wallet feature to select models. More vehicles are expected to be added over time. Eligible customers will receive notifications in the “What’s New” section of their vehicle’s app when digital-key support is available. Users will be able to use their smartphones or Apple Watches much like a physical key to unlock their vehicles. GM mentioned supported vehicles will automatically unlock as a driver approaches and lock as the driver walks away. According to the tech giant, the vehicle’s trunk and climate control system will be accessible with the new Apple Wallet feature. “The digital key experience will continue to evolve beyond simply unlocking and starting a vehicle. By leveraging ultra-wideband technology, GM is laying the groundwork for more deeply integrated and personalized experiences like automatically adjusting vehicle settings as drivers approach and other intelligent features that make ownership more convenient,” said the company in a press release. Apple first announced the concept at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2020. It later launched exclusively for select 2021 BMW 5 Series models. Since then, the tech company has added other major automakers, such as Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, and Audi, to the offering. The digital key may work even when a phone’s battery is dead. The company said that depending on a user’s iPhone model, keys could still be available even when a device needs to be charged. However, it warned that they will be available only for up to five hours. The evolution of digital keys Samsung rolled out its own version of the digital keys in 2021. In October, Samsung announced it would support digital keys for select GM vehicles. The digital key is the latest evolution in car-key technology. In the 1980s, automakers began using radio frequencies to create remote keyless entry fobs. In 2008, Nissan and tech company Sharp launched a mobile phone with a built-in intelligent car-key chip in Japan. Then, in 2017, Tesla advanced the concept by making its smartphone app the primary, default key for the Model 3, replacing the standard physical key fob. Apple and GM did not immediately respond to requests for comment. AI-generated videos are becoming an key part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how rapidly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Recent findings suggest that video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

The most commonly used formats include:.

It has been revealed that for most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Industry observers note that resolution is an vital factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:.

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Sources indicate that frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Sources indicate that designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially notable for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:.

Sources indicate that compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Sources indicate that bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

In a recent development, trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Recent findings suggest that removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Sources indicate that even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:.

A simple implementation looks like this:.

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Industry observers note that technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract owners or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

It has been revealed that mobile compatibility is equally crucial. Smaller screens, limited data aims, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

According to recent reports, AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that one of the ideas I’m always trying to tell my students is that their brains are something, an asset, if you like, they need to protect.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of the ideas I’m always trying to tell my students is that their brains are something, an asset, if you like, they need to protect. The human brain is an amazing optimizer: Provide it with an effortless way to achieve something, and it will rapidly start to use it. We used to memorize a ton of phone numbers a few decades ago. Now we can hardly memorize our own, simply because our brain knows the number is a few clicks away. A clear example is why I never use AI to write my articles: simply because, for me, in my personal methodology as a professor of innovation, writing is my way of making concepts stick in my brain, concepts I will need later to teach and discuss. If I ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or any other chatbot to write my articles for me, I would lose much of the learning that writing gives me. This doesn’t mean I don’t use AI: I can use it to translate certain parts, to search for relevant articles to back up an assertion, or to assess whether the concepts I try to explain come across clearly. But I don’t want to use it for writing, because writing is a skill I want to protect. And like a muscle, if you don’t exercise it, it quickly atrophies. For a manager, the skill worth protecting might be decision-making: An AI that makes every choice could undermine precisely the judgment that person needs to develop. The useful behavior depends on the objective, and sometimes that objective requires the system to hold back. What happens when we move from personal to corporate use? Can an AI learn when its intervention would make things worse? That capability might receive very little applause in a product demonstration, but it could be enormously valuable in practice. The sales agent that lets us be  Imagine a firm using a sales agent. When it identifies a customer approaching renewal, it follows a standard procedure: It quickly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount, and schedules a follow-up. All of it in mere seconds. And the audience claps enthusiastically. But what if our customer would have renewed anyway? Then, the end result is that we have wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer, and surrendered margin unnecessarily. What if our customer is a happy one, and the right thing to do would have been just to wait for him or her to renew voluntarily? Even when all tasks are perfectly executed, the decision to perform them could have been perfectly wrong. The cost of being helpful We know how this feels when we’re working with real people: Experienced employees often develop a sense of when to follow up, when to escalate an issue, and when making too many interventions will look messy, send the wrong signal, or make the customer upset. How do they know that? It comes with experience; it’s learning that compounds over time, with more and more iterations. That judgment is something we pay to have. However, when we evaluate AI, we tend to be fascinated with visible activity—with messages generated, tasks completed, workflows executed, etc. The equivalent is if we were dealing with a hyperactive employee. And as we probably know, someone who sends twice the number of messages is probably not twice as valuable. In other words, just because an action can be automated and, therefore, performed easily, doesn’t mean that we should be performing it all the time. Look what happens with AI coding assistants: In “When to show a suggestion? Integrating human feedback in AI-assisted programming,” Microsoft researchers used data from 535 programmers to retrospectively evaluate a system that selectively withheld suggestions that were apparently likely to be rejected by the developers. They also found that optimizing for suggestion acceptance could produce lower-quality suggestions. Getting people to accept more assistance was an imperfect measure of helping them. Learning when to intervene In the case of our renewal agent, a system that learns from a lot of comparable cases could perhaps investigate which interventions help with whom. For instance, some customers don’t like the feeling of being “directed” or “influenced,” and are better left to their own devices. Some like a particular type of interaction through a particular channel, but they hate others. Or they want to talk to the same customer representatives every time because they remember them. The function to protect would be the ability to spot these cases. Do not automate; optimize. But optimization is not necessarily something that today’s corporate AI does well. Today’s corporate AIs can generate splendid emails, but following the before and after and deciding to do nothing is usually not an alternative. It’s the experience from all previous cases, processed along with the specific characteristics of every customer, that leads to the lessons learned, to the continuous improvement, to the process being optimized. And that ability to improve decisions through accumulated experience is precisely what you need. Give waiting a fair chance When buying or deploying AI, managers should, therefore, find out what outcome the system is theoretically trying to improve, and design ways to know whether its actions helped or not. We need to be honest here: A renewal following an email does not necessarily establish that the email was the reason for the renewal. Customers differ, circumstances change, and useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. Simply storing more interaction histories will not settle the question. This includes maintaining the necessary human oversight, the now-famous “human-in-the-loop”: A missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. People must define the obligations and limits within which the system can learn. I haven’t seen an AI system that reviews an account, checks all the available evidence from the corporate ERP or CRM, and decides that contacting the customer would probably make things worse. So the final outcome would be that nothing gets sent, no discount is offered, and we just let the customer evolve naturally. No hyperactivity. Why? Because our corporate learning optimized it, and the accumulated learning behind that decision should remain under our company’s control, available even if we replace the model or the vendor powering our agents. It might be a disappointing demo. But it could be excellent business.

One of the ideas I’m always trying to tell my students is that their brains are something, an asset, if you like, they need to protect. The human brain is an amazing optimizer: Provide it with an effortless way to achieve something, and it will quickly start to use it. We used to memorize a ton of phone numbers a few decades ago. Now we can hardly memorize our own, simply because our brain knows the number is a few clicks away.

According to recent reports, A clear example is why I never use AI to write my articles: simply because, for me, in my personal methodology as a professor of innovation, writing is my way of making concepts stick in my brain, concepts I will need later to teach and discuss. If I ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or any other chatbot to write my articles for me, I would lose much of the learning that writing gives me.

This doesn’t mean I don’t use AI: I can use it to translate certain parts, to search for relevant articles to back up an assertion, or to assess whether the concepts I try to explain come across clearly. But I don’t want to use it for writing, because writing is a skill I want to protect. And like a muscle, if you don’t exercise it, it swiftly atrophies.

Sources indicate that for a manager, the skill worth protecting might be decision-making: An AI that makes every choice could undermine precisely the judgment that person needs to develop. The useful behavior depends on the objective, and sometimes that objective requires the system to hold back.

What happens when we move from personal to corporate use? Can an AI learn when its intervention would make things worse? That capability might receive very little applause in a product demonstration, but it could be enormously valuable in practice.

Imagine a organization using a sales agent. When it identifies a customer approaching renewal, it follows a standard procedure: It promptly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount, and schedules a follow-up. All of it in mere seconds. And the audience claps enthusiastically.

Recent findings suggest that but what if our customer would have renewed anyway? Then, the end result is that we have wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer, and surrendered margin unnecessarily. What if our customer is a happy one, and the right thing to do would have been just to wait for him or her to renew voluntarily?

Even when all tasks are perfectly executed, the decision to perform them could have been perfectly wrong.

According to recent reports, we know how this feels when we’re working with real people: Experienced employees often develop a sense of when to follow up, when to escalate an problem, and when making too many interventions will look messy, send the wrong signal, or make the customer upset. How do they know that? It comes with experience; it’s learning that compounds over time, with more and more iterations.

That judgment is something we pay to have. However, when we evaluate AI, we tend to be fascinated with visible activity—with messages generated, tasks completed, workflows executed, etc. The equivalent is if we were dealing with a hyperactive employee. And as we probably know, someone who sends twice the number of messages is probably not twice as valuable.

And that ability to improve decisions through accumulated experience is precisely what you need.

Customers differ, circumstances change, and useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. Simply storing more interaction histories will not settle the question.

According to recent reports, this includes maintaining the necessary human oversight, the now-famous “human-in-the-loop”: A missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. People must define the obligations and limits within which the system can learn.

Jeff Bezos’s $41 billion AI startup Prometheus is shrouded in secrecy. We found out who’s building it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for many in the tech industry, physical AI is the next world to conquer.
  • According to recent reports, for many in the tech industry, physical AI is the next world to conquer.
  • Sources indicate that the promise is enormous.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for many in the tech industry, physical AI is the next world to conquer. While developers of large language models like OpenAI and Anthropic seek to push reasoning models distilled on billions of streams of text to their limits, an emerging crop of companies are focusing on an even more ambitious goal: developing AI programs designed to speak the language of physics. Should they succeed, these firms have a stake in everything from building models that might power self-driving manufacturing or enable drug discovery to those that can take on plane design and weapons development. The promise is enormous. Whoever cracks physical AI could control a slice of the software stack that becomes critical to a host of industries—and worth many, many billions. Already, a growing list of companies are racing to stake their claim. Among the buzziest is Prometheus, a startup backed by Jeff Bezos that’s already flush with cash. Bezos isn’t just bankrolling Prometheus. He’s also coleading the manufacturer, marking his first executive role since stepping down as Amazon’s CEO in 2021. His cofounder is Vik Bajaj, a Stanford professor who previously led science operations at Verily, Alphabet’s health technology venture. Prometheus was incubated in 2024 at Foresite Labs, which Bajaj leads, with support from the venture capital firm Arch Venture Partners. A number of Prometheus employees also appear to have come from firms associated with Bajaj. By combing through LinkedIn and researchers’ personal websites, Fast Company identified 130 people who say they’re currently working for Prometheus, and assembled what appears to be the first public database of its kind. Prometheus employs approximately 250 people, including numerous accomplished AI researchers, some of whose names have not been publicly disclosed. The company is recruiting not only AI model developers but also experts in fields like aerospace and chemistry, a strong hint that it may one day target manufacturing and healthcare customers. Employees bring expertise in ocean engineering, energy engineering, mathematics, and even high-performance computing. In this Subscriber Exclusive, you’ll discover: An exclusive database of the more than 130 people who have publicly joined Prometheus, Bezos’s buzzy and secretive AI startup What those employees’ expertise tells us about where the company is headed, and direct insights from people within Prometheus about what they’re actually building A list of rival companies competing in the physical AI space—and their investors Deep insight into what physical AI actually is, and why the market could be worth hundreds of billions Why Bezos’s other, more renowned companies, Amazon and Blue Origin, stand to benefit most if Prometheus succeeds At a Semafor event on November 17, Bezos and Bajaj noted they’ve spent much of their funding on compute and have built one single multi-physics model. Thus far, Prometheus has built a neural surrogate for numerical simulation and has used the technology to design a range of hardware, including an experiment that involved having the company’s models redesign the Mars helicopter. This next AI revolution needs AI tools trained not on text but on data from the physical world, as well as subject-matter experts who can ensure that models are distilling a common core of engineering principles that can extend across myriad domains. This, in turn, involves recruiting not just AI coders but plenty of people with expertise in the physical realm, whether that’s manufacturing automotive parts or running biology labs. “Most fundamentally, the biggest challenge is just the sheer breadth of what we’re doing. Engineering is vast. There’s no such thing as an engineer,” one leading AI expert and early-stage Prometheus employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, tells Fast Company. “This idea of building something that’s general enough to cover all of that space, that’s been a really, really huge challenge—and a really interesting one.” What Prometheus, and physical AI, aim to achieve News that Prometheus (formerly called the Prometheus Project) was under development went public only last year, and its leadership has been tight-lipped about what it’s actually trying to build. We do know that the company was incubated at Foresite Labs, which is housed within the health and life sciences investment firm Foresite Capital. (In addition to Prometheus, Foresite Labs has backed companies like AI drug discovery startup Xaira and disease therapy outfit Alumis.) Still, Prometheus’s bare-bones website includes only links to its LinkedIn and X pages, and government documents show that Prometheus used a code name (“FL2024-008 INC”) for a small amount of lobbying and when applying for H1-B visas for some employees. We also know that Prometheus has attracted significant capital from investors interested in healthcare, AI, and tech manufacturing. The company originally raised about $6 billion in funding, and then another $12 billion—for a $41 billion valuation—earlier this year. Its backers, Semafor reported in June, include JPMorgan; BlackRock; and Arch Venture Partners. Other backers include Powerlaw, a closed-end fund that has also invested in high-tech companies like SpaceX, Colossal, and Waymo, as well as RoboStrategy, a venture capital fund that states it owns shares in the company. Bezos has said that the company isn’t focused on robotics, though that’s what many people first associate with the term physical AI. Instead, Prometheus aims to develop what it calls an artificial general engineer, which Bezos likens to a much more advanced version of computer-aided design, or CAD, powered by artificial intelligence. “My through line for the last few years has been AI,” Bezos said in an interview with Squawk Box anchor Andrew Ross Sorkin earlier this year. “My time at Amazon is spent on AI. My time at Prometheus is spent on AI—Prometheus is really an AI company. And my time at Blue [Origin] is largely spent on AI. And [at] Prometheus . . . the tools that we’re building are going to help companies like Blue immensely.” A trademark application makes clear that Prometheus’s aspirations extend far beyond healthcare, spanning much of the engineering and manufacturing pipeline. The document references physical simulations and digital twin technology, along with structural, thermal, fluid, acoustic, and electromagnetic analysis, and even “acoustic and vibration analysis, noise prediction, and acoustic design optimization.” The application also discusses 3D printing, semiconductor manufacturing, and developing factory layouts. It’s not hard to see why this interdisciplinary approach might one day prove lucrative. Companies spend an extraordinary amount of time researching and developing upcoming components and hardware, a process that can involve the arduous work of finding and vetting suppliers. There’s also the expensive, resource-intensive process of simulating and testing how new systems perform once they’re built and under different conditions. Another challenge: developing production lines capable of manufacturing that hardware at scale. Consider the development of a jet engine, a process that can require thousands of workers and more than a decade of design, prototyping, testing, and manufacturing. Prometheus envisions AI tools that could dramatically compress that timeline, from, say, a decade to just a few years. The company sees similar opportunities across everything from household products to large-scale industrial systems. The aspiration for the physical AI industry is to automate as much of the process as possible and make real-world testing and evaluation far more efficient. The idea is that this could speed up hardware development across a wide range of industries. Indeed, Prometheus reportedly already has its eyes on a network of spin-offs in which it might one day own stakes. “Today it takes days to weeks for engineers to set up one simulation for one design. There are a lot of repetitive, manual, low-added-value tasks that they have to go through while using this software,” explains Thomas von Tschammer, cofounder of Neural Concept, a physical AI startup and Prometheus competitor. “The opportunity with AI is first of all to automate and compress a lot of this low-added-value work from those engineers so that they can actually spend time engineering.” Inside Prometheus One early Prometheus employee, an expert in neural networks who was among the company’s first hires, was excited to “get back to basics” and pursue fundamental research. At the Bezos-backed firm, the employee says he’s working on building an “end-to-end” system at the intersection of physics and AI, developing “accurate, high-fidelity simulations” that could help engineers with initial designs. The goal, the employee says, is to create an agentic artificial engineer that could one day drive “simulations and use them to make design decisions at the highest level.” Such an AI system would ideally be generalizable across engineering disciplines, much as current LLMs can be applied to a wide range of text-based tasks and types of content. “If we can get a tool that across many different domains is able to simulate faster and more accurately, you can see how this generalizes to fields that wouldn’t otherwise have had contact very much at all,” the Prometheus employee says. A good number of staffers come from other major AI companies, including xAI, and many have particular experience in AI-based materials science. Notably, a number hail from companies where Bajaj was formerly affiliated, including Google, Foresite Labs, and Foresite-backed Xaira. Before leaving Foresite, Bajaj helped incubate a range of biotech firms and filed a patent for AI-based nucleic acid sequencing. Several employees have also come to Prometheus from General Agents, the applied AI research lab that Prometheus quietly acquired last year. The lab released “Ace,” a real-time computer autopilot, last year, and its former CEO, Sherjil Ozair, is now on Prometheus’s technical staff. Other staffers have far more eclectic backgrounds. In its quest to build powerful simulations, Prometheus has hired at least one former employee of video game developer Epic Games, and a former AI researcher from Meta’s Reality Labs. The company has also recruited employees from Waymo and Red Bull Advanced Technologies, which helps translate Formula 1 innovations into applications for the automotive and aerospace industries. Prometheus’s hires also suggest that it may eventually want to sell to the government. The company’s team includes a technical adviser who also serves as a chief scientist for the U.S. Army’s ground systems research. Another Prometheus adviser is Chase Johnson, who previously served in the Marine Corps’ innovation unit and worked as an attorney for defense tech company Anduril. Johnson, in his LinkedIn bio, suggests Prometheus could one day transform the “defense industrial base.” Another employee who works at Prometheus government relations tells Fast Company that what brought them to the Bezos-backed firm was the desire to work on “cutting-edge” problems. In particular, they’re interested in how an AI engineering agent could aid industries with critical supply chains, including the automotive and semiconductor sectors. “We are entirely focused on building models and products for the physical economy, and to accelerate the dream to build loop,” the employee says. “We are exclusively focused on design, engineering, and manufacturing, and I think that is an advantage. Focus is always an advantage, and we know that we are purpose-built for design, engineering, and manufacturing.”  The quest for physical AI Bezos may already have a ready-made customer for Prometheus: himself. His space company, Blue Origin, is developing reusable rockets to launch satellites and humans into orbit, with ambitions that extend to orbital data centers. (At that Semafor event, Bezos said Blue Origin was already using some Prometheus tech.) All of that requires extensive manufacturing and engineering work, which could benefit from the kind of AI-powered software Prometheus is developing. Bezos has acknowledged the potential connection, though it remains unclear whether—or how—Prometheus might ultimately integrate with his other businesses. Then there’s Amazon, which does plenty of its own in-house manufacturing, maintains frontier AI and robotics research groups, and has invested heavily in warehouse robotics. Bezos has also invested in Physical Intelligence, a startup developing AI models for the physical world and robotics, though there doesnt’ appear to be any formal relationship between the two companies. Taken together, these interests raise the possibility that Bezos is positioning himself to build a new, far-reaching empire centered on physical AI. In the meantime, a range of other startups are competing in the physical AI race. Anima Anandkumar and Benedikt Jenik were once approached about leading Prometheus before launching their own startup, Accelerated Understanding. (That offer, Reuters previously reported, came from Bajaj and would have included a major stake in the company and a million-dollar salary.) Their focus is on building models capable of making predictions in four dimensions, at any resolution. To do that, they say they need a team that isn’t constrained by traditional disciplinary silos or the limitations of conventional LLMs. “Even if one were to use LLMs to automate execution, the real world stays the bottleneck,” Anandkumar tells Fast Company. “If we instead teach AI models to directly simulate and understand physics, that bottleneck goes away.” Other firms envision a similar formula for building physical AI teams: a mix of machine learning generalists and specialists with engineering and manufacturing experience. Paul Eremenko, of P-1 AI, which makes an agentic AI tool called Archie that works directly within engineering teams, argues that it’s often much easier to train someone with an aerospace background in the latest AI research than to teach an AI specialist the nuances of aerospace engineering. “We don’t compete with OpenAI or Anthropic for talent,” Eremenko says. “The prototypical AI researcher or AI engineer for us is somebody who comes from a physical world background—a mechanical engineer, aerospace engineer, electrical engineer—who became very interested in AI.” Back at Prometheus, the competition for talent is only expected to intensify. An employee working in government relations tells Fast Company that the Prometheus expects to expand its workforce exponentially, even as hiring remains highly selective. For the early employee specializing in AI, the recruiting pitch comes down to the opportunity to tackle problems that have long eluded conventional engineering tools. “In terms of wooing them, I think I’m often selling people on the novelty and the excitement.”.

The tech giant has also recruited employees from Waymo and Red Bull Advanced Technologies, which helps translate Formula 1 innovations into applications for the automotive and aerospace industries.

Prometheus’s hires also suggest that it may eventually want to sell to the government. The manufacturer’s team includes a technical adviser who also serves as a chief scientist for the U.S. Army’s ground systems research. Another Prometheus adviser is Chase Johnson, who previously served in the Marine Corps’ innovation unit and worked as an attorney for defense tech company Anduril. Johnson, in his LinkedIn bio, suggests Prometheus could one day transform the “defense industrial base.”.

It has been revealed that another employee who works at Prometheus government relations tells Fast Company that what brought them to the Bezos-backed firm was the desire to work on “cutting-edge” problems. In particular, they’re interested in how an AI engineering agent could aid industries with critical supply chains, including the automotive and semiconductor sectors.

“We are entirely focused on building models and products for the physical economy, and to accelerate the dream to build loop,” the employee says. “We are exclusively focused on design, engineering, and manufacturing, and I think that is an advantage. Focus is always an advantage, and we know that we are purpose-built for design, engineering, and manufacturing.”.

Recent findings suggest that bezos may already have a ready-made customer for Prometheus: himself. His space tech giant, Blue Origin, is developing reusable rockets to launch satellites and humans into orbit, with ambitions that extend to orbital data centers. (At that Semafor event, Bezos said Blue Origin was already using some Prometheus tech.) All of that requires extensive manufacturing and engineering work, which could benefit from the kind of AI-powered software Prometheus is developing. Bezos has acknowledged the potential connection, though it remains unclear whether—or how—Prometheus might ultimately integrate with his other businesses.

Industry observers note that then there’s Amazon, which does plenty of its own in-house manufacturing, maintains frontier AI and robotics research groups, and has invested heavily in warehouse robotics. Bezos has also invested in Physical Intelligence, a startup developing AI models for the physical world and robotics, though there doesnt’ appear to be any formal relationship between the two companies. Taken together, these interests raise the possibility that Bezos is positioning himself to build a new, far-reaching empire centered on physical AI.

In the meantime, a range of other startups are competing in the physical AI race. Anima Anandkumar and Benedikt Jenik were once approached about leading Prometheus before launching their own startup, Accelerated Understanding. (That offer, Reuters previously reported, came from Bajaj and would have included a major stake in the company and a million-dollar salary.) Their focus is on building models capable of making predictions in four dimensions, at any resolution. To do that, they say they need a team that isn’t constrained by traditional disciplinary silos or the limitations of conventional LLMs.

It has been revealed that “Even if one were to use LLMs to automate execution, the real world stays the bottleneck,” Anandkumar tells Fast Company. “If we instead teach AI models to directly simulate and understand physics, that bottleneck goes away.”.

Other firms envision a similar formula for building physical AI teams: a mix of machine learning generalists and specialists with engineering and manufacturing experience.

Paul Eremenko, of P-1 AI, which makes an agentic AI tool called Archie that works directly within engineering teams, argues that it’s often much easier to train someone with an aerospace background in the latest AI research than to teach an AI specialist the nuances of aerospace engineering.

Recent findings suggest that “We don’t compete with OpenAI or Anthropic for talent,” Eremenko states. “The prototypical AI researcher or AI engineer for us is somebody who comes from a physical world background—a mechanical engineer, aerospace engineer, electrical engineer—who became very interested in AI.”.

Back at Prometheus, the competition for talent is only expected to intensify. An employee working in government relations tells Fast Company that the Prometheus expects to expand its workforce exponentially, even as hiring remains highly selective. For the early employee specializing in AI, the recruiting pitch comes down to the opportunity to tackle problems that have long eluded conventional engineering tools. “In terms of wooing them, I think I’m often selling people on the novelty and the excitement.”.

#34772. Tech Report: Anthropic’s IPO asks investors to bet that a product can build a firm, not the other way around

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1477 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Anthropic’s IPO asks investors to bet that a product can build a firm, not the other way around

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Anthropic releases its initial public offering this Thursday, it will be another test of how much further the AI industry’s seemingly unchecked growth can go.
  • When Anthropic debuts its initial public offering this Thursday, it will be another test of how much further the AI industry’s seemingly unchecked growth can go.
  • But the IPO also asks investors to make a more unusual bet: on a company whose own product could eventually do much of the work of building the business itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Anthropic releases its initial public offering this Thursday, it will be another test of how much further the AI industry’s seemingly unchecked growth can go. The company is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion, asking investors to buy into the idea that artificial intelligence will become a major contributor to the economy. But the IPO also asks investors to make a more unusual bet: on a company whose own product could eventually do much of the work of building the business itself. In its amended S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, released last week, Anthropic claims that “each fresh version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next.” Claude already helps run experiments, generate training data, and test future models, the company says. As evidence, Anthropic notes that Claude wrote more than 90% of contributions to its code base in September 2026. In the three-month period through September, the daily volume of code contributed per engineer was more than 45 times its 2024 average. Traditionally, companies go public asking investors to bankroll employees who will build and sell better products. Anthropic is pitching something different: a business whose products increasingly help develop their own successors—and, in the process, help build the company itself. There is some precedent for a company using its own technology to improve it. When the software company GitLab went public in 2021, its prospectus described how employees used GitLab’s development platform to identify problems and determine what to build next, a practice known as “dogfooding.” But that was software helping human developers do their jobs, rather than AI increasingly performing the work itself. “It may be the first IPO in which this type of thing is happening,” says Sinan Aral, a professor at MIT Sloan School of Management. Still, Aral cautions against confusing AI’s growing role in developing products with the ability to decide which products should exist in the first place. Claude may be writing code, but humans remain responsible for the more consequential research decisions. “What to do, what goals to have and what to optimize, is generally being decided by human beings,” he says. Even so, experts say Anthropic’s pitch represents a striking departure from the conventional IPO. Until now, discussions of recursive self-improvement—the idea that AI systems could improve their own capabilities—have largely centered on the risks of systems becoming misaligned with human goals, says Jay Ritter, director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. But Ritter sees a potentially transformative business opportunity, too. Unlike conventional processes of innovation, which often yield diminishing returns, AI-driven self-improvement could theoretically produce exponential gains. That would fundamentally change not only how products are developed, but how the companies behind them operate. “Anthropic and its competitors are companies that are increasingly capable of building themselves,” Ritter says. “Investors are essentially being asked to pay for the electricity to do this.” The prospect also raises questions about how much autonomy Anthropic is willing to grant Claude—and whether a system capable of directing its own development would make decisions aligned with human interests. For now, MIT’s Aral says, the company appears reluctant to surrender that control. Its S-1 contains “a risk section like we’ve never read before,” he says, reflecting the possibility that its technology could eventually begin making consequential decisions on its own. Not everyone is convinced that such a future is imminent, or even plausible. Kirill Skrygan, CEO of JetBrains, a company known for its software development tools, is skeptical that Anthropic has created an AI system capable of improving itself without human intervention. He also disputes the notion that Anthropic represents an entirely new kind of business, one whose development could eventually escape human control. “I think it’s more about hype before the IPO,” he says. Indeed, a closer reading of Anthropic’s filing reveals a more qualified vision than its headline figures might suggest. The company acknowledges that errors in existing models could carry over into future ones, and says it does not expect to let Claude develop successive frontier models without meaningful human supervision—at least not yet. Whether Anthropic can deliver on its vision of AI increasingly building the business behind it remains an open question. Investors who buy the stock this week will be betting that it can, even as the company itself acknowledges the risks and limitations of that ambition.

The best kids’ gifts of 2026 are all about screen-free calm

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past decade, waking up on Christmas morning with kids involved a cacophony of beeping robots, singing plush toys, and gadgets flashing every color of the rainbow.
  • Over the past decade, waking up on Christmas morning with kids involved a cacophony of beeping robots, singing plush toys, and gadgets flashing every color of the rainbow.
  • It has been revealed that for years, toy makers have packed their products with tech designed to keep kids engaged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past decade, waking up on Christmas morning with kids involved a cacophony of beeping robots, singing plush toys, and gadgets flashing every color of the rainbow. (Until somebody quietly “lost” the batteries.) For years, toy makers have packed their products with tech designed to keep kids engaged. Tablets autoplayed the next episode, and apps were engineered to keep kids hooked. But parents have had enough, especially after a growing pile of research has linked heavy screen use to all kinds of problems in children. Families are now hunting for ways to help their kids slow down and regulate their nervous systems. But there’s a growing consensus among scientists and developmental psychologists that the problem isn’t technology itself; it’s that companies are engineering these devices to addict kids. And a fresh generation of toy designers is flipping the script. They’re incorporating technology to calm kids down, rather than rev them up, swapping out feeds and autoplays for calming music and stories. This new “quiet tech” movement has produced some of the most innovative products on the market. For this year’s guide, I rounded up my favorite examples of gifts that soothe instead of overstimulate. Most are completely screen-free. I’ve arranged them to follow the arc of a kid’s day, from the first yawn to lights out. Your own nervous system may thank you, too. [Source image: Skylight] Getting Out the Door Without a MeltdownSkylight, Skylight Buddy, $139.99 (plus $39 per year for Buddy Plus after the first free month) In many homes, mornings are incredibly stressful, as parents struggle to get kids to do the most basic tasks to get out the door on time. Skylight Buddy was created to solve this problem. It’s a small bedside device featuring a friendly character that walks kids through their morning, after-school, and bedtime routines. Buddy is also an alarm clock, a night-light, and a white noise machine that shuts off on its own in the morning. Its OK-to-wake light changes color so a kid knows they can get out of the room and wake the rest of the family up. The optional Buddy Plus blueprint adds star rewards, a visual timer, and messages from parents that Buddy reads aloud. It’s designed for ages 4 to 10. [Source image: Charmspring] The Calm of Knowing What Happens NextCharmspring, SpringboardGo Large, $95 Research demonstrates that kids feel calmer when they know what’s coming next in their day. Charmspring’s SpringboardGo is a magnetic board that maps out a child’s day and week, with 194 magnetic tiles that show different tasks and activities, like “brush teeth” and “school.” Kids can help create the schedule, which helps them feel empowered. It’s a lighter, more compact version of the brand’s original Springboard, so it fits in smaller spaces. It also arrives in gift-ready packaging, which is one less thing to wrap. [Source image: Dex] Say BonjourDex, Dex Language-Learning Camera, $249 Dex is a kids’ camera that doubles as a language tutor. Kids point it at everyday objects (an apple, a passing fire truck), and Dex will translate the word into the language they’re learning. If they snap a picture of the object, it adds more details like color, shape, and what the thing does. Dex covers 16 languages and more than 30 dialects, from Spanish and Mandarin to Hindi and Arabic, with levels from beginner to advanced. It has a small touchscreen, but the whole point is to get kids looking up at the world. It’s designed for ages 3 to 8. [Source image: Parcel Air] No Opening Until Wheels UpParcel Air, Airplane Box, $68 Flying with kids can be a nightmare. Most parents resort to handing them a tablet and declaring unlimited screen time. But Parcel Air’s boxes are designed to create hours of screen-free entertainment for short and long-haul flights. Each box holds four hand-numbered parcels wrapped in kraft paper and twine. Kids open them one at a time, and only once the plane is in the air. The boxes come in four age ranges, from 2 and under up to 8. The Navigator, for ages 6 to 8, includes a gear-building machine, an explorer’s book, group trivia, and a rocket to build on the descent. Younger kids get magnetic blocks, crafts, and finger puppets. (Road-tripping instead? The Carpool box, from $38, is filled with toys that won’t scatter across the back seat.) [Source image: Piccalio] A beautiful spot to do activitiesPiccalio, Arcc Kids Table & Chair Set, from $469 Calm kids need a quiet space in the home to come back to. Piccalio’s new Arcc set, designed by the celebrated furniture designer Hanne Willmann, aims to give little ones their own spot for drawing, puzzles, and snack time. While many play tables are painted in primary colors and emblazoned in cartoon characters, this set takes its cues from 1970s Scandinavian modernism. It’s made of bent beech plywood with soft arches and rounded edges, and it comes in beech, walnut, tomato, or powder blue. It’s also Montessori inspired, which means the furniture is scaled to a child’s body so they can climb in and get to work on their own. It’s a splurge, from $469 for a table and one chair up to $999 for four chairs. But it’s handsome enough that you won’t mind it in the living room or kitchen. It’s available for preorder. It’s designed for ages 3 to 6. [Source image: Super Smalls] Small Beads, Substantial CalmSuper Smalls, Make It Yummy Mini Bead Kit, $22 There’s something very soothing about threading beads onto a string, one at a time. Super Smalls, founded by the former fashion magazine editor Maria Dueñas Jacobs, makes some of the most charming bead kits around. My favorite is the Make It Yummy mini kit that comes in a palm-sized box with food-related beads and three charms (an egg, a slice of pizza, and a donut), plus enough stretchy cord for a necklace and a bracelet, or three bracelets. It’s a perfect stocking stuffer. If food isn’t your thing, it comes in plenty of other themes, including fruit, rainbows, ocean, outer space, and a Make It Mazel version with Jewish charms like a chai and a hamsa. Kids who catch the bug can graduate to the Super Entrepreneur Bead Kit ($75), which has more than 630 beads, 25-plus charms, and jewelry cards and stands so they can set up their own shop. Designed for ages 3 and up. [Source image: Tonies] Screen Free GamingTonies, Tonieplay Games, $24.99 each; Tonieplay Controller, $14.99 (requires Toniebox 2, from $139.99) The Toniebox, the beloved cube that plays stories when kids set a figurine on top, has a new trick. The latest version of the device allows kids to play screen-free games. Thanks to clever design, the games operate on audio commands and a small dial-shaped controller that allows kids to make choices or select answers. This year, Tonies teamed up with Hasbro to create audio versions of three classics: The Game of Life, Guess Who? and Monopoly. Kids can play by themselves or with others. [Source image: Cali] The Book That Reads AlongCali, Cali Reader + 3 Stories, $99 Cali Reader looks and feels like a real book but, like magic, it reads stories aloud to kids. The child begins by snapping a 32-page paper storybook (like The Three Little Pigs or Winnie-the-Pooh) into the reader and pressing the pages to hear the story read aloud as they follow along. Each book comes with three games and word-recognition activities designed by educators, so it can help children build reading skills. In a small pilot study, first graders who used it made bigger gains in phonics, fluency, and vocabulary than a control group. Designed for ages 3 to 6. [Source image: Yoto] Lights Out, Story OnYoto, Yoto Player 4th Gen, $149.99 The Yoto has become a fixture of the screen-free bedroom, and this fall the organization released a major upgrade. Kids still pop in cards to play audiobooks, music, and podcasts. But a new Green Button lets them operate a custom playlist, like a morning music mix or a bedtime wind-down, without having to plug in a particular card. There’s also a new full-panel night light that glows in seven colors and doubles as an OK-to-wake light. The player holds more than 1,000 hours of audio for offline listening. For kids on the go, the smaller Yoto Mini 4th Gen ($109.99) is now splash- and dust-resistant. Designed for ages 3 and up.

It has been revealed that this year, Tonies teamed up with Hasbro to create audio versions of three classics: The Game of Life, Guess Who? and Monopoly. Kids can play by themselves or with others.

The Book That Reads AlongCali, Cali Reader + 3 Stories, $99.

Industry observers note that cali Reader looks and feels like a real book but, like magic, it reads stories aloud to kids. The child begins by snapping a 32-page paper storybook (like The Three Little Pigs or Winnie-the-Pooh) into the reader and pressing the pages to hear the story read aloud as they follow along. Each book comes with three games and word-recognition activities designed by educators, so it can help children build reading skills. In a small pilot study, first graders who used it made bigger gains in phonics, fluency, and vocabulary than a control group. Designed for ages 3 to 6.

Lights Out, Story OnYoto, Yoto Player 4th Gen, $149.99.

The Yoto has become a fixture of the screen-free bedroom, and this fall the company released a major upgrade. Kids still pop in cards to play audiobooks, music, and podcasts. But a new Green Button lets them operate a custom playlist, like a morning music mix or a bedtime wind-down, without having to plug in a particular card. There’s also a new full-panel night light that glows in seven colors and doubles as an OK-to-wake light. The player holds more than 1,000 hours of audio for offline listening. For kids on the go, the smaller Yoto Mini 4th Gen ($109.99) is now splash- and dust-resistant. Designed for ages 3 and up.

This farming game is designed to keep you off your phone

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that there’s one way to win the smartphone game Island: Screen Time Control.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s one way to win the smartphone game Island: Screen Time Control. You have to stay off your phone. The makers of the gamified screen time blocker are betting that a different approach to smartphone time management can yield better long-term results. The goal of Island: Screen Time Control is growing virtual crops to sell for digital coins. Crops grow over time, and you can sell them to a boat that arrives once a day. With more money, you can begin to upgrade your island with fresh crops, trees, flowers, and other features. [Image: SideKit] The founders of SideKit, which made the app, say the typical approach of nannying screen time or adding friction doesn’t really work. “Most screen time apps use a formula of set limits and a wall that reveals up when you exceed them,” SideKit CEO Ashish Selvaraj tells Fast Company. That friction doesn’t change habits, Selvaraj says. Ethan Pronev and Ashish Selvaraj [Photo: SideKit] “We believe that there is no level of wall ‘hardness’ that can change your behavior long term,” he says. “As long as you outsource your self-regulation, you won’t be able to see lasting change.” For their app, Selvaraj and SideKit CTO Ethan Pronev, who met while attending the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, took inspiration from idle games and their most addictive UI features. The app begins with an onboarding process that asks you to remember the last short-form video you watched and the last time you closed your phone and felt like it was time well spent. From there, you’re taken to your island, a tiny plot of land where you start with 50 coins (cucumbers, for example, cost 20 coins to plant). You’re asked to share your screen time, then set your own limits for your selected app categories. A screen time bar on the left side of the game shows how close you’ve come to hitting a limit. The more you stick to your time limits, the better the weather is on your island, which creates a bigger harvest. [Image: SideKit] Instead of logging into your problem apps, you can log into the game and check how your crops are doing and harvest them when they’re ready. The gamified aspect provides a dopamine hit you might get from TikTok or Instagram notifications or infinite scroll, and there are other built-in features that reward you for keeping your limits—but not so many that you’ll spend too much time in the app. A focus timer is built into a boat offshore that you can click to turn your phone into a timer; it catches fish the longer you’re on it. A credit system improves your credit score every day that you stick to your limits, giving the app its own streak-tracking feature. The app is free, but there’s a pro subscription for $5.99 per month or $39.99 per year that gives you access to features such as per-app time limits and “soul link” mode, so you and a friend can keep each other even more accountable as both islands suffer if one of you spends too much time on your phone. The approach is carrot over stick, using positive reinforcement instead of nagging to encourage owners to engage in behaviors that help their island and crops. SideKit says it’s working: Over the 18,400 days of data the company has, it says users stopped at or below their set limit 82% of the time. “Who doesn’t love a farming game?” Selvaraj says.
