  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, the best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says.
  • According to recent reports, to compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, the best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

According to recent reports, to compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

In a recent development, humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

It has been revealed that quillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Industry observers note that pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

It has been revealed that custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

It has been revealed that pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Industry observers note that grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship reveals which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the prepares page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid looks also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Sources indicate that undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ claims pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid intends start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

According to recent reports, variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Pricing: Free on Ahrefs' website.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

It has been revealed that there isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

#34765. Industry News: How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students

Industry News: How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.
  • Jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.
  • In a recent development, they interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce. They interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers. Finance firms came and ran affinity information sessions and job shadowing programs for first- and second-year students. “They would specifically say: ‘We’re looking for BIPOC students. We’re looking for first-gen students. We’re looking for LGBTQIA+ students,’” mentioned Chambers, executive director of the school’s Hameetman Career Center. Not anymore. Those pipelines, Chambers said, have “dried up.”  After a divided Supreme Court gutted race-conscious admissions in 2023, colleges could no longer give an edge to Black and Latino applicants over white and Asian applicants in the name of diversity, ushering in a new era for higher education. That meant the end of policies aimed at turning around historically low representation and systemic discrimination. The court’s ruling—which more than two-thirds of American adults told Gallup was “mostly a good thing”—did not address or change hiring laws nor mention employer efforts to make workplaces more inclusive. Yet many employers have since dismantled existing efforts to recruit diverse workers on college campuses, reporting by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions found. Tech giant leaders removed or revised diversity language, changed recruitment strategies and reconsidered how they built pools of candidates, according to a Columbia Business School study based on a survey of human resources professionals. Half of those surveyed who were familiar with the ruling mistakenly believed it applied to workplaces; others feared becoming a target of lawsuits, public criticism, or political attention. They’re facing a hostile atmosphere. In January 2025, as one of the first acts of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order that attacked so-called diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) hiring programs across federal agencies and contractors. Calling these efforts “discriminatory and illegal,” the order also pressured private employers to follow suit—including publicly traded corporations, large nonprofits, and universities with major endowments. Fear of drawing Trump’s ire appears to be the major reason many private employers have removed racial and gender representation goals from their hiring pipelines. Conservative legal activists used the Supreme Court ruling on affirmative action at colleges as a road map for targeting workplace programs that prioritize diversity. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, urged businesses to remove or revoke corporate DEI positions, warning state and federal governments not to contract with corporations that have such statements. The full impact the ban on affirmative action at colleges will have on job placement won’t be known until 2028, once the first class of college students admitted since the decision graduates and enters the workforce. But one of the starkest consequences of both the court ruling and the pressures of the second Trump administration is already clear, as colleges and workplaces alike retreated from promises to fight racism and injustice through bolstered diversity programs that they made after the 2020 murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer. “I feel like this is clearly a backlash to that moment,” said Natasha Warikoo, a sociology professor at Tufts University who has studied affirmative action, noting that previously, a focus on racial justice “felt like a moral imperative.” Bryan J. Cook, director of higher education policy in the Work, Education, and Labor Division at the Urban Institute, said what he sees so far in early workforce trends is concerning, although he added that the midterm election’s sweeping verdict on Trump “could have some impact.” With Democrats controlling the House and Senate, he said, “It will be interesting to see if Congress pushes back on the administration’s anti-DEI efforts, including some to the DOJ investigations into schools’ admissions practices.” More than three dozen major companies contacted for this story—among them Meta, Google, Walmart, Target and Goldman Sachs—declined to discuss their recruiting practices, a stark contrast to companies’ previously publicized efforts to diversify their workforces. In addition, dozens of colleges approached for interviews would not make their career staff available or did not respond. Several counselors agreed to talk only if neither they nor their schools were named, citing concern about drawing the attention of the Trump administration. Following the court’s decision, Black enrollment declined or remained flat at nearly all highly selective private and public colleges—the 85 that accept 25% or less of applicants—and the same was true of Hispanic enrollment at more than half of those institutions. For example, at Harvard University, one of the defendants in the Supreme Court case, the percentage of incoming students who are Black has fallen by nearly half since 2023. That year, they made up 18% of the first-year class, while in 2026, they’re just 9.3%. Meanwhile, the path to the most prestigious entry-level jobs is also narrowing to favor students from a smaller set of largely private elite colleges—places where the entering classes are becoming less diverse, said Matt Sigelman, president of The Burning Glass Institute, a labor research firm. Before the decision, when companies and recruiters had broader diversity goals, they were casting a wider net, Sigelman said. And though the court decision was about college admissions, employers “could see the writing on the wall and changed the way they were hiring.” They put together guidance they were getting from the Department of Labor along with changes in the political culture, said Sigelman, and “in many cases pulled back from their diversity goals.’’ Burning Glass looked at the careers of 300,000 college graduates who entered the workforce between 2023 and 2025 to understand who landed where, and specifically who got jobs at the most competitive companies. Over that period, the share of those hires coming from the most elite colleges rose by nearly a third, according to the firm’s research, which typically draws on large databases of online career profiles, such as those on LinkedIn, and job postings. The results suggest that landing a good first job increasingly depends on which college a student gets into, and Sigelman thinks first-generation and minority students will remain at a particular disadvantage if they aren’t already known to employers. “What started as a decision about who gets admitted to college ultimately plays out in who gets a shot at the best employment,” Sigelman said. Other research on recruiting points yields similar findings. While nearly 60% of 150 major employers identified diversity as a priority for determining where to send campus recruiters in 2022, that figure was down to 31% in 2025, according to a survey by Veris Insights, a recruiting research firm. Over the same period, the share of major companies recruiting exclusively from a short list of schools rose from 17% to 26%, the survey found. There are also early signs that internships—an key employment pipeline for college students—are becoming more difficult for minority students to obtain, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers, which connects college career offices with the employers that recruit from them. The association tracks the makeup of corporate internship programs, one of the main pipelines that companies used to diversify their workforce. It found that from 2021 to 2024, white students made up 50% to 53% of those interns. In the cohort that ran from fall 2024 through summer 2025, spanning Trump’s return to office, that share rose to 59%, said Shawn VanDerziel, the association’s president and CEO. He added that the weak job market, artificial intelligence, and inflation make it difficult to interpret this trend. California had already banned race-based affirmative action in public university admissions in 1996, with lasting consequences for students’ education and economic prospects, studies found. Still, recruiters regularly visited California’s campuses seeking out students of color, first-generation students, and women in science and engineering. But now, at the University of California, Berkeley, Santina Pitcher, senior associate director of employer relations, said federal agencies “from the Peace Corps to the State Department” have told her they can no longer explicitly recruit for diversity. Recruiters “weren’t approaching us in the same way” at Pomona College after the court ruling, said Hazel Raja, associate dean and senior director of the career development office on the private campus in Claremont, California. “My assumption is that there was a little bit of everybody pulling back to begin with, and then reassessing ways that they could still diversify their workforce in ways that still allowed for them to stay above the law in light of the policy changes,” Raja said. At San Jose State University, where more than 40% of students are the first in their families to attend college, the career center renamed some programs soon after the federal government changed its guidance in response to Trump’s executive order. References to DEI disappeared. What was once called a diversity job fair has been renamed the October Fest job and internship fair, said Lisa Trikofski, assistant director of employment engagement at the campus career center.Students say they can feel a shift underway. At San Jose State last spring, students moved through a career fair with résumés and rehearsed handshakes, navigating booths for companies that were looking to recruit. Winnie Tuban, who is Filipino and first in her family to go to college, said she enrolled at the school because it sits at the center of the design world she wanted to enter in Silicon Valley, close to headquarters for several tech company giants. Apple, Google, Meta, Adobe and Zoom recruited San Jose State graduates over the years and hired scores of them. Tuban has since graduated and ultimately found a job at a small startup in San Francisco on her own, not through recruiters. She said she found the landscape discouraging. “I feel like regardless of where you stand politically, when you’re living as a person of color and you hear that they’re ‘going to war on DEI,’ it makes it feel like you’re not welcome in that space,” she said. Daniella Mensah, a psychology major, was 2 when her family immigrated from Ghana. That idea, Hess said, “far too often seems to have been reduced to counting the number of people from a particular race or ethnic group.”  In his view, real diversity would also mean hiring people from different regions, social classes, religions, and political outlooks. “Businesses can’t pretend that selecting employees based on skin color is a good proxy for all of the rich differences that they say they want to attend to,” he said. Now, she is having conversations with her own children that echo the conversations her parents had with her, in a very different era. “It is a challenge,” she said. “But we’re up for it.” This story was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.

In a recent development, they interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers. Finance firms came and ran affinity information sessions and job shadowing programs for first- and second-year students.

Recent findings suggest that “They would specifically say: ‘We’re looking for BIPOC students. We’re looking for first-gen students. We’re looking for LGBTQIA+ students,’” said Chambers, executive director of the school’s Hameetman Career Center.

Not anymore. Those pipelines, Chambers said, have “dried up.”.

It has been revealed that after a divided Supreme Court gutted race-conscious admissions in 2023, colleges could no longer give an edge to Black and Latino applicants over white and Asian applicants in the name of diversity, ushering in a fresh era for higher education. That meant the end of policies aimed at turning around historically low representation and systemic discrimination.

The court’s ruling—which more than two-thirds of American adults told Gallup was “mostly a good thing”—did not address or change hiring laws nor mention employer efforts to make workplaces more inclusive.

Yet many employers have since dismantled existing efforts to recruit diverse workers on college campuses, reporting by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions found.

Tech giant leaders removed or revised diversity language, changed recruitment strategies and reconsidered how they built pools of candidates, according to a Columbia Business School study based on a survey of human resources professionals. Half of those surveyed who were familiar with the ruling mistakenly believed it applied to workplaces; others feared becoming a target of lawsuits, public criticism, or political attention.

They’re facing a hostile atmosphere. In January 2025, as one of the first acts of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order that attacked so-called diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) hiring programs across federal agencies and contractors.

Calling these efforts “discriminatory and illegal,” the order also pressured private employers to follow suit—including publicly traded corporations, large nonprofits, and universities with major endowments.

Fear of drawing Trump’s ire appears to be the major reason many private employers have removed racial and gender representation goals from their hiring pipelines. Conservative legal activists used the Supreme Court ruling on affirmative action at colleges as a road map for targeting workplace programs that prioritize diversity.

The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, urged businesses to remove or revoke corporate DEI positions, warning state and federal governments not to contract with corporations that have such statements.

The full impact the ban on affirmative action at colleges will have on job placement won’t be known until 2028, once the first class of college students admitted since the decision graduates and enters the workforce. But one of the starkest consequences of both the court ruling and the pressures of the second Trump administration is already clear, as colleges and workplaces alike retreated from promises to fight racism and injustice through bolstered diversity programs that they made after the 2020 murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer.

“I feel like this is clearly a backlash to that moment,” said Natasha Warikoo, a sociology professor at Tufts University who has studied affirmative action, noting that previously, a focus on racial justice “felt like a moral imperative.”.

According to recent reports, bryan J. Cook, director of higher education policy in the Work, Education, and Labor Division at the Urban Institute, remarked what he sees so far in early workforce trends is concerning, although he added that the midterm election’s sweeping verdict on Trump “could have some impact.” With Democrats controlling the House and Senate, he said, “It will be interesting to see if Congress pushes back on the administration’s anti-DEI efforts, including some to the DOJ investigations into schools’ admissions practices.”.

More than three dozen major companies contacted for this story—among them Meta, Google, Walmart, Target and Goldman Sachs—declined to discuss their recruiting practices, a stark contrast to companies’ previously publicized efforts to diversify their workforces.

Industry observers note that in addition, dozens of colleges approached for interviews would not make their career staff available or did not respond. Several counselors agreed to talk only if neither they nor their schools were named, citing concern about drawing the attention of the Trump administration.

Following the court’s decision, Black enrollment declined or remained flat at nearly all highly selective private and public colleges—the 85 that accept 25% or less of applicants—and the same was true of Hispanic enrollment at more than half of those institutions.

According to recent reports, for example, at Harvard University, one of the defendants in the Supreme Court case, the percentage of incoming students who are Black has fallen by nearly half since 2023. That year, they made up 18% of the first-year class, while in 2026, they’re just 9.3%.

Meanwhile, the path to the most prestigious entry-level jobs is also narrowing to favor students from a smaller set of largely private elite colleges—places where the entering classes are becoming less diverse, remarked Matt Sigelman, president of The Burning Glass Institute, a labor research firm.

Before the decision, when companies and recruiters had broader diversity goals, they were casting a wider net, Sigelman mentioned. And though the court decision was about college admissions, employers “could see the writing on the wall and changed the way they were hiring.”.

They put together guidance they were getting from the Department of Labor along with changes in the political culture, said Sigelman, and “in many cases pulled back from their diversity goals.’’.

Burning Glass looked at the careers of 300,000 college graduates who entered the workforce between 2023 and 2025 to understand who landed where, and specifically who got jobs at the most competitive companies.

Over that period, the share of those hires coming from the most elite colleges rose by nearly a third, according to the firm’s research, which typically draws on large databases of online career profiles, such as those on LinkedIn, and job postings.

The results suggest that landing a good first job increasingly depends on which college a student gets into, and Sigelman thinks first-generation and minority students will remain at a particular disadvantage if they aren’t already known to employers.

“What started as a decision about who gets admitted to college ultimately plays out in who gets a shot at the best employment,” Sigelman remarked.

It has been revealed that other research on recruiting points yields similar findings. While nearly 60% of 150 major employers identified diversity as a priority for determining where to send campus recruiters in 2022, that figure was down to 31% in 2025, according to a survey by Veris Insights, a recruiting research firm. Over the same period, the share of major companies recruiting exclusively from a short list of schools rose from 17% to 26%, the survey found.

There are also early signs that internships—an important employment pipeline for college students—are becoming more difficult for minority students to obtain, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers, which connects college career offices with the employers that recruit from them.

The association tracks the makeup of corporate internship programs, one of the main pipelines that companies used to diversify their workforce. It found that from 2021 to 2024, white students made up 50% to 53% of those interns.

According to recent reports, in the cohort that ran from fall 2024 through summer 2025, spanning Trump’s return to office, that share rose to 59%, noted Shawn VanDerziel, the association’s president and CEO. He added that the weak job market, artificial intelligence, and inflation make it difficult to interpret this trend.

It has been revealed that california had already banned race-based affirmative action in public university admissions in 1996, with lasting consequences for students’ education and economic prospects, studies found. Still, recruiters regularly visited California’s campuses seeking out students of color, first-generation students, and women in science and engineering.

But now, at the University of California, Berkeley, Santina Pitcher, senior associate director of employer relations, stated federal agencies “from the Peace Corps to the State Department” have told her they can no longer explicitly recruit for diversity.

Recruiters “weren’t approaching us in the same way” at Pomona College after the court ruling, stated Hazel Raja, associate dean and senior director of the career development office on the private campus in Claremont, California.

“My assumption is that there was a little bit of everybody pulling back to begin with, and then reassessing ways that they could still diversify their workforce in ways that still allowed for them to stay above the law in light of the policy changes,” Raja said.

It has been revealed that at San Jose State University, where more than 40% of students are the first in their families to attend college, the career center renamed some programs soon after the federal government changed its guidance in response to Trump’s executive order. References to DEI disappeared.

At San Jose State last spring, students moved through a career fair with résumés and rehearsed handshakes, navigating booths for companies that were looking to recruit. The price of success nobody warns founders about: Who are you after you sell your company?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal.
  • We entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal.
  • Yet almost nobody teaches us how to live after the exit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal. Yet almost nobody teaches us how to live after the exit. In 2008, I did what most entrepreneurs dream of doing. I exited the business I’d spent nearly two decades building, just before the global financial crisis. By almost any measure, it was a remarkable success. What I discovered, and what I want to share with my fellow entrepreneurs, is that no one tells you about the psychological consequences of success. We celebrate the exit as the ultimate achievement: the culmination of years of sacrifice, sleepless nights, and relentless determination. A liquidity event takes place and the founder collects the check and disappears into a life of freedom and fulfilment. That’s the narrative, anyway. But my experience was very different, because my identity was fully linked to my business and everything it represented. I didn’t recognize it then, but I’d confused what I did with who I was. Without the business, I wasn’t entirely sure who I was anymore, and almost overnight my identity disappeared. What I’ve come to find out is that this is much more common than you may think it is. The hidden cost of no exit plan I built my property advisory business, Ober-Haus, after arriving in Estonia in the early 1990s, and developed it into a company that operated across seven countries. For nearly 20 years, my life revolved around building, negotiating, financing, and solving problems. I loved it and became good at it. Then I sold the company. Suddenly, I had the financial freedom I’d only dreamed about and spent most of my adult life pursuing—but that was when things began to unravel. Years before building Ober-Haus, I’d confronted alcoholism, entered recovery, and rebuilt my life. Yet I hadn’t fully recognized how easily the compulsive drive that once fueled my drinking could find a more socially celebrated outlet: ambition and success. After my exit, I moved to Argentina and immersed myself in a world of horses, polo, travel, and an extraordinary lifestyle. From the outside, it looked like the perfect reward for decades of hard work. Parts of it were wonderful, but something fundamental was missing. I’d spent so long pursuing financial independence that I hadn’t seriously considered what I would do with it once I had it. The adrenaline of building a business had been replaced by the pleasures of spending the proceeds. What I mistook for freedom was, in some ways, another form of escape. And the purpose of life disappeared slowly until finally it was gone. Over time, my wealth diminished. My marriage collapsed. I made difficult financial decisions and watched much of what I’d accumulated disappear. The exit that was supposed to secure my future became the beginning of one of the most difficult periods of my life, and came with a hidden cost that I’d never considered. A darker side to success Looking back, I can see that the problem began long before I sold my company. Entrepreneurs develop qualities that help us succeed: drive, competitiveness, resilience, an appetite for risk, and an almost obsessive determination to achieve our goals. These characteristics can build extraordinary businesses, but they don’t necessarily build extraordinary lives. We become accustomed to controlling outcomes, solving problems and measuring progress. We approach relationships like negotiations and personal fulfilment like another business objective. When something isn’t working, our instinct is to push harder or cut our losses. Success demands sacrifice; we accept that almost without thinking, whether it’s another missed family dinner, another canceled holiday, or another year promising ourselves that life will slow down after the next transaction. But there comes a moment when success starts asking for something we’re no longer willing to give. Our health. Our integrity. Our relationships. Perhaps even our sense of self. And the question becomes whether we can keep going without betraying ourselves further. This is the dark side of success that is rarely discussed—the problem with getting everything we ever wanted. Not because entrepreneurs don’t experience it, but because admitting it feels dangerously close to admitting failure. The answer isn’t another achievement When my life began falling apart, my instinct was familiar: start another business. I’ve done just that with a property credit business in the U.K., which restored direction, confidence, and financial purpose. What’s different this time around, however, is that I’ve come to understand that rebuilding a business and rebuilding a life are two different things. One can be measured in revenues, assets and returns. The other requires questions that don’t fit neatly into a spreadsheet: Who am I without the title? What do I actually want? Which relationships have I neglected? What am I still trying to prove, and to whom? These are uncomfortable questions for people accustomed to having answers, which is how many entrepreneurs operate. Yet avoiding them simply postpones the reckoning. It’s been hard to face this, especially when you consider that we live in a culture obsessed with optimization. We’re encouraged to extend our peak, maximize performance, preserve our youth, and constantly reinvent ourselves. While there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, sometimes this optimization becomes a sophisticated way of avoiding harder questions about identity, relationships, integrity and purpose. A changed relationship with success I want to share my story because I suspect there are thousands of successful founders wrestling with the question of who they are after the exit. From the outside, they appear to have everything. Inside, they’re wondering what happened. Today, in my sixties, I’m still an entrepreneur, still ambitious, and still interested in creating things. But the fundamental difference this time around is that my relationship with success has changed. I’m beginning to understand that my next chapter isn’t necessarily about becoming the version of the person I used to be—it’s about letting go of the person I no longer need to be. Contrary to what all the books and courses and stories tell you, the hardest part of success isn’t reaching the top. It’s actually when you discover that the person you became to get there is no longer the person you want to be. So if you’re an entrepreneur in a similar position, I invite you to consider the idea that your identity is more than your business achievements, and to then find the courage to build a life that doesn’t require you to keep climbing.

Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters, and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Flock, in particular, operates a nationwide camera network, with data from cameras operated in one jurisdiction frequently accessed by investigators from elsewhere, making it hard for local officials to understand and control privacy risks. As a result, while Flock and other providers emphasize that their cameras have been used to investigate legitimate crimes, rescue kidnapped kids, and track stolen cars, many municipalities have ended their contracts, in some cases even covering cameras awaiting removal by the service provider. Many businesses deploy their own automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, to track vehicles in their parking lots, sometimes sharing that information with law enforcement. But since private companies aren’t subject to freedom of information laws, it can be hard to know which businesses have them and what they’re doing with the data they collect. To help people understand in time for the holiday shopping season which stores use the devices, Fight for the Future just released a scorecard listing 10 major retailers and what the organization knows about their use of the cameras. “Retailers also need to be brought into the conversation,” says Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at Fight for the Future, which previously organized a campaign with home improvement influencers that called on Home Depot and Lowe’s to cut ties with Flock. The chart is based on information the organization received from a questionnaire sent to the retailers and, in cases where they didn’t respond, third-party news reporting, crowdsourced camera spotting, and information from published privacy policies. “We got responses from just a handful of [businesses],” Suleiman says. The exact details vary, and many businesses don’t appear to use the technology at every location. Costco, for instance, told Fight for the Future that it uses ALPR cameras at “less than a dozen locations nationwide,” so it’s difficult to know just from the checklist whether your local branch of a national chain is equipped with the cameras. But it’s easy to see at a glance that many major brands at least acknowledge in their privacy policies that they might be using the technology. Some stores also indicate that they may share information from the devices with law enforcement. The scorecard offers links to retailers’ emails, along with suggested text, to ask them to refrain from using ALPR technology, even if (or perhaps especially if) the details about how they do so may be opaque. Fight for the Future also encourages people to reach out with any tips about retailers that are using the cameras or with requests to add particular stores to the scoresheet. “We don’t have a FOIA request that we can do for companies or a public records act request that we can impose upon companies, but nothing’s stopping us from writing to them,” Suleiman says. “Nothing’s stopping people from letting these companies know what they want and what they expect.”.
